\chapter{Family}
\label{ch:russian-family}
\hlchaptermodality{8}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name a family in Russian, and say what its own root shares with the English word home.}

A one-lesson chapter that gathers Chapter 7's four people under \ru{семья}, and reaches all the way back to Chapter 3's \ru{жить} to rescue that lesson's stranded etymon — the two words share an idea, if not a root, and the chapter says so honestly.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[sem'yá]{\ru{семья} — \textquotedblleft{}family,\textquotedblright{} the word that gathers the chapter before it}

\label{lesson:RU-C08-semya}



\begin{quote}
One word to hold everyone Chapter 7 introduced — and a root that turns out to be hiding an English word you use every day.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — \ru{семья}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ru{семья}} — \emph{sem'yá} — \textbf{family}
\end{quote}

The soft sign softens the \textbf{\ru{м}}; stress lands on the final \textbf{-\ru{я}}, so it rhymes with \emph{\ru{друг} · \ru{подруга} · \ru{брат} · \ru{сестра}} — this is the word that gathers all four of them.

\emph{(Note the ending: \textbf{-\ru{ья}} is a soft-consonant variant of \textbf{-\ru{я}}, and still counts as the regular feminine ending from Chapter 6's rule.)}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ru{семья}} is Indo-European *\emph{\'{k}ey-}, \textquotedblleft{}to lie down, to settle\textquotedblright{} — the same root that, through the Baltic branch, gave Lithuanian \textbf{šeimà}, \textquotedblleft{}family,\textquotedblright{} and Ancient Greek \textbf{kōmē}, \textquotedblleft{}village.\textquotedblright{} That is already a wide family. But it goes one branch further: through \textbf{Proto-Germanic *haimaz}, \textquotedblleft{}home, village,\textquotedblright{} the very same root became English \textbf{home} — and, in its diminutive form, \textbf{hamlet} — and it survives fossilized in every English place name ending in \textbf{-ham}: \emph{Birmingham}, \emph{Nottingham}, \emph{Durham}. Settle somewhere, and Slavic calls the people you settled with your \emph{\ru{семья}}; the deep Germanic cousin of that same root calls the place itself your \emph{home}.

Chapter 3 taught you \textbf{\ru{жить}}, \textquotedblleft{}to live\textquotedblright{} — a different root (PIE *\emph{g\textsuperscript{w}eyh\textsubscript{3}-}, the one behind English \emph{quick} in its old sense of \textquotedblleft{}alive\textquotedblright{}), but the same idea from a different angle: \textbf{\ru{семья}} is who you settle with; \textbf{\ru{жить}} is what you do once you're there.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\ru{семья}\textquotedblright{} — soft \ru{м}, stress on -\ru{я}
  \item the four it gathers — \textquotedblleft{}\ru{друг}, \ru{подруга}, \ru{брат}, \ru{сестра} — \ru{моя} \ru{семья}\textquotedblright{} in idea, if not yet in Russian grammar
  \item the cousin — \textquotedblleft{}\emph{\'{k}ey-} settle $\to$ \ru{семья}, and $\to$ home, hamlet, -ham\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\ru{семья}, \ru{жить}\textquotedblright{} — who you settle with, and what you do there
\end{itemize}
